title: throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-wip-12
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures the current throughput benchmarking harness and methodology we use for serving-runtime investigations. It covers harness architecture, load generator configs, warmup/repeatability requirements, metrics to collect, and common pitfalls. This is a working doc (WIP) — use as the canonical place for test recipes and reproducibility guidance until we move to the dedicated Confluence page.

Goals:
- Provide repeatable, low-noise throughput measurements across model variants, quantization modes, and hardware profiles.
- Make it easy for engineers to compare relative changes (PRs, kernel swaps) and measure end-to-end tokens/sec and latency SLOs.
- Ensure we capture production-relevant behavior: batching dynamics, cache/KV effects, and autoscaling interactions.

High-level harness architecture (notes):
- Controller: orchestrates experiments, config templating, and result aggregation. Typically a Python CLI (redwood-loadrunner) that accepts a YAML test spec.
- Load generators (LGen): distributed workers that issue inference requests. Lightweight, single-threaded process per CPU core to reduce coordination noise.
- Collector: central Prometheus pull endpoint + sidecar that collects host/GPU counters, plus a per-request trace log for sampled requests.
- Artifact store: experiment metadata, run outputs (raw logs, aggregated CSVs), and a pointer to the exact code/commit + container image used.

Test isolation and reproducibility checklist (must-haves for each run):
- Commit SHA: record serving-runtime and model-serving images used.
- Container image tag and digest (e.g., gcr.io/redwood/serving:sha-abc123).
- Hardware profile: GPU model, driver version, CUDA/cuDNN versions.
- Node config: CPU governor, NUMA settings, cgroups used, hugepages.
- Environment flags: TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST, OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS.
- Deterministic seeds where applicable: random prompt generation seeds, tokenizer seeds.
- Network topology: on-host vs remote LB, loopback vs cross-node.

Load generator config knobs (recommended fields in YAML test spec):
- name: descriptive id
- model: model name + server endpoint
- model_variant: float32|int8|q4_0 etc.
- input_distribution: fixed_prompt|random_prompts_from_corpus|uniform_len
- prompt_seed: integer for reproducibility
- sequence_length: avg_tokens, max_tokens, or distribution spec (we prefer sampling from production-ish histogram)
- request_pattern: open_loop|closed_loop (open loop = fixed QPS, closed loop = concurrency-limited)
- target_qps: for open_loop tests
- concurrency: for closed_loop tests (number of outstanding requests)
- batch_profile: prefer explicit batch sizes or let runtime auto-batching; when explicit, specify batch_sizes and mix ratios
- warmup_duration: seconds (see warmup section)
- run_duration: seconds of steady-state measurement window
- grace_periods: pre- and post-run quiesce windows for metrics exporter
- headers/metadata: route, api_key, model_version pinned
- sampling_rate: fraction of requests to record full trace (default 0.01)

Warmup and steady-state guidance:
- Warmup rationale: JIT compilation, kernel selection, scheduler warm paths, and KV cache behavior cause throughput to ramp up. If you measure too early you'll underestimate steady-state tokens/sec.
- Recommended warmup: 3x the model typical latency or a fixed floor (min 120s) for complex models. For small testbeds, at least 60s. For production-scale runs, 300s warmup is safe.
- Warmup pattern: start with low QPS (10-20% target), ramp linearly to target over warmup_duration to avoid spikes that trigger autoscaling.
- Steady-state window: discard first 20% of post-warmup results, then measure for run_duration (recommend 600s for stable percentile estimates).
- Repeat runs: run at least 3 independent trials with a short cool-down (2*P99 latency) between them. Use the median across trials as canonical.

Open-loop vs closed-loop recommendations:
- Open-loop (fixed QPS): best for measuring raw system capacity and kernel-level throughput because it decouples client pacing from server latency. Use when evaluating maximum tokens/sec under saturation.
- Closed-loop (fixed concurrency): best for latency SLO studies since it simulates a limited client concurrency pattern. Good for p95/p99 behavior under load.
- For end-to-end benchmarking, run both: open-loop to find saturation point, then closed-loop at target concurrency to validate SLOs.

Metrics to collect (per-run):
- Client-side: request_count, success_rate, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), tokens_per_request, requests_per_second (rps), tokens_per_second.
- Server-side: per-model queue length, batch sizes observed, GPU utilization (util%), GPU memory used (MiB), SM occupancy, kernel launch counts, CPU user/sys, scheduler queue time.
- System: network tx/rx, disk IO (if caching), host load average, process-level thread counts.
- Detailed traces: sampled request traces showing timeline: request recv, routing, batch wait time, kernel execution start/end, response send.

How to interpret results / signal vs noise:
- Use tokens/sec normalized to a fixed tokenization (e.g., byte-pair tokenization spec + vocabulary). Always report tokens/sec and requests/sec along with avg tokens/request.
- Prefer median of multiple runs; report min/median/max for throughput and p95/p99 latencies to show variability.
- If GPU utilization is <70% at expected throughput, investigate kernel-level inefficiencies (small batch sizes, divergent sequence lengths).
- If p99 is much larger than p95 (e.g., 3x), look for tail causes: autoscaling events, GC, host preemption, thermal throttling, or batch imbalance.

Profiler integration and bottleneck triage:
- Run NVTX-instrumented builds and capture Nsight Systems for targeted runs to see kernel timelines and host-side stalls.
- Capture per-kernel timings and aggregate by op type (attention, ff, layernorm). Compare expected FLOPs to runtime to estimate kernel efficiency.
- Use CUPTI metrics to get achieved occupancy, memory throughput, and identify memory-bound kernels.
- Correlate with host perf counters (context switches, syscalls) to find CPU-side bottlenecks (e.g., copying, serialization, tokenizer).

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Non-deterministic prompt generation: always pin seed or use canned corpora for comparisons.
- Background noise: run on isolated nodes, disable cron jobs, and use dedicated NICs.
- Docker layering differences: ensure image digest stable. Clean caches between runs when testing cold-start behavior.
- Autoscaler interference: disable autoscaling for controlled runs or pin capacity. If testing autoscaler, treat it as a separate experiment and collect scaling events.

Example test YAML (template):
---
name: bert-large-8k-qps-test
model: bert-large
model_variant: q4_0
input_distribution: corpus_sample
prompt_seed: 42
sequence_length: {avg: 128, max: 512}
request_pattern: open_loop
target_qps: 500
batch_profile: {allow_auto: true, preferred_batch_sizes: [8,16,32]}
warmup_duration: 180
run_duration: 600
concurrency: null
sampling_rate: 0.02
---
(We store full run outputs under artifacts/<run-id>/ and include metadata.json with image digests and commit SHAs.)

Quick CLI examples (redwood-loadrunner):
- Discover model: redwood-loadrunner list-models --env perf
- Run open-loop: redwood-loadrunner run --spec tests/bert-qps-500.yaml --out runs/2026-01-12-bert-qps-500
- Aggregate results: redwood-loadrunner analyze --runs runs/2026-01-12-bert-qps-500 --output csv

Result reporting conventions:
- Always include: model name + variant, hardware, image digest, commit SHA, warmup strategy, open/closed loop type, tokens/sec (median), p50/p95/p99 (ms), batch size distribution.
- Visuals: time-series tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, kernel timeline heatmap for the representative run.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Add a dedicated job in CI that runs a quick smoke throughput test on PRs (30s warmup, 120s run) against a tiny model to catch regressions.
- Standardize artifacts naming and retention policy (keep last 90 days + tagged golden runs).
- Integrate more systematic tokenization histograms sampled from production to create realistic input distributions.
- Expand the collector to include CUPTI-derived metrics automatically.

Notes to self / open questions:
- How much do we want to emulate multi-tenant noise in CI vs keep CI tests very clean? My inclination: CI = clean determinism; nightly jobs = noisy/production-like.
- Should we add a synthetic adversarial prompt generator to stress kernel memory patterns?

End of doc.
